note.explanation: To measure liquid volume, place the measuring cylinder on a horizontal surface and read the meniscus at eye level. For water, read the bottom edge of the meniscus. To find the volume of a solid that does not dissolve, compare the liquid reading before and after immersing it. If the solid is too large for the cylinder, use a displacement can and measure the overflow.
examples: If the water level rises from 20 mL to 32 mL after a solid is immersed, the solid’s volume is 32 mL − 20 mL = 12 mL.
If a solid does not fit in a measuring cylinder, collect the overflow from a displacement can and measure it with a measuring cylinder.
note.checkAnswer: Read the bottom edge of the water meniscus with your eye level with it.
note.simple: Read the water level straight on, at the bottom of its curved surface. A solid’s volume is the amount of water it displaces.
note.checkQuestion: When reading the volume of water in a measuring cylinder, which edge of the meniscus should you read?
note.title: Measuring the volume of liquids and solids
steps: Place the measuring cylinder on a horizontal surface.
Bring your eye level with the water meniscus.
Read the scale at the bottom edge of the water meniscus.
To find a solid’s volume, subtract the initial liquid reading from the reading after the solid is immersed.
If the solid does not fit in the cylinder, collect the overflow from a displacement can and measure it in a measuring cylinder.
note.answer: For water, read the volume at the bottom edge of the meniscus, with your eye level with it.

mcqs.stem: Which instrument is designed to measure the volume of liquids and non-dissolvable solids?
rationales: Correct: a measuring cylinder is a graduated cylinder used to measure liquid volume and the volume of non-dissolvable solids.
A balance measures mass, not volume.
A ruler measures length, not volume.
A can without a scale cannot directly give a volume reading.

At the bottom edge of the water meniscus

mcqs.stem: Where should the volume of water be read in a measuring cylinder?
rationales: The top edge is used for a convex mercury surface, not the concave surface of water.
Correct: the reading for water is taken at the bottom edge of its concave surface.
The book’s method specifies the bottom edge, not the middle.
The reading must correspond to the correct edge of the meniscus.

mcqs.stem: How should the eye be positioned to read a measuring cylinder correctly?
rationales: Looking down at the meniscus gives an incorrect reading.
Looking up at it also gives an incorrect reading.
Correct: the eye should be level with the meniscus to avoid a viewing-angle error.
Moving the eye does not provide a reliable reading.

mcqs.stem: What should you do with a measuring cylinder before taking a volume reading?
rationales: Correct: the cylinder should be placed on a horizontal surface for a correct reading.
An angled cylinder can make the liquid level and scale reading unreliable.
Holding the cylinder can tilt it and disturb the reading.
A sloping surface does not provide the required level position.

options: Read the initial level only
Read the level after immersion only
Subtract the initial reading from the reading after immersion
Add the two readings
mcqs.stem: How is the volume of a non-dissolvable solid found by immersing it in liquid in a measuring cylinder?
rationales: The initial reading alone is the liquid’s volume before the solid is added.
The final reading includes both the liquid and the displaced volume, so it is not the solid’s volume alone.
Correct: the increase in the liquid reading equals the volume of the immersed solid.
Adding the readings does not give the volume of the solid.

options: A solid that dissolves in the liquid

A liquid whose volume is already known

mcqs.stem: When is a displacement can especially useful for measuring a solid’s volume?
rationales: A dissolving solid changes the liquid and is not suitable for the displacement method described.
Correct: the section recommends a displacement can when the body does not fit into the measuring cylinder.
A displacement can is not needed simply because a liquid’s volume is known.
Floating does not by itself make the solid too large for the cylinder.

The body’s mass

mcqs.stem: In the displacement can method, what is collected in a beaker and measured with a measuring cylinder?
rationales: Correct: the overflowing liquid is collected and measured; its volume equals the solid’s volume.
The method measures volume, not mass.
The method does not require measuring the can’s capacity.
The method does not measure the body’s height.

options: Water curves upward, so its top edge is read
Water curves downward, so its bottom edge is read
Water has no meniscus

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the correct reading of water in a measuring cylinder?
rationales: Water curves downward; a top-edge reading is not the method given for water.
Correct: water has a concave surface that curves downward, and the reading is taken at its bottom edge.
Water has a meniscus, which is the top level of the liquid surface.
The eye should be level with the meniscus, not below the cylinder.

written.text: Why is it difficult to locate the meniscus in a wider vessel?
written.finalAnswer: The meniscus is less curved and flatter in a wider vessel, so its edge is harder to locate.

yourTurn.question:
When using a measuring cylinder, one precaution to take is to:
(a) check for the zero error
(b) look at the meniscus from below the level of the water surface
(c) take several readings by looking from more than one direction
(d) position the eye in line with the bottom of the meniscus
solution: For water, the reading is taken at the bottom edge of the meniscus.
The eye should be level with that bottom edge.
Therefore, the correct answer is (d) position the eye in line with the bottom of the meniscus.
yourTurn.answer: (d) position the eye in line with the bottom of the meniscus.

hints: The method measures a change in liquid level caused by a solid.
The collected overflow has a volume equal to the immersed solid’s volume.
yourTurn.question:
A displacement can is used to measure:
(a) mass of a liquid
(b) mass of a solid
(c) volume of a liquid
(d) volume of a solid
solution: A solid immersed in a displacement can pushes liquid out through the side opening.
The overflow is collected and measured in a measuring cylinder.
The volume of the overflow equals the volume of the solid.
Therefore, the correct answer is (d) volume of a solid.

steps.why: The first reading records the liquid’s volume before the solid is added.
The higher reading includes the volume displaced by the immersed solid.
steps.text: Reading after the solid is immersed = 32 mL

steps.why: The increase in the reading is the volume of the solid.
steps.text: Volume of the solid = 32 mL − 20 mL

steps.why: Subtracting the readings gives the volume displaced by the solid.

explain.title: Measuring cylinder
explain.body: “It is a cylinder made of glass or transparent plastic with a scale divided in cubic centimetres (cm³ or cc) or millilitres (mL) marked on it. It is used to find the volume of liquids and non-dissolvable solids.” Place it on a horizontal surface and read the liquid level at eye height.

explain.title: Meniscus and reading water
explain.body: “The meniscus is the top level of the liquid surface.” Water curves downward and its surface is called concave. For water, take the reading at the bottom edge of the surface. Mercury curves upward, making a convex surface, so take its reading at the top edge.

explain.title: Volume by displacement
explain.body: Note the liquid reading before and after placing a non-dissolvable solid in it. The difference between the readings is the solid’s volume. If the body does not fit in the measuring cylinder, use a displacement can: collect the overflowing liquid and measure it in a measuring cylinder. That volume equals the solid’s volume.

explain.title: Avoid a wrong reading
explain.body: Keep the cylinder level on a horizontal surface. Keep your eye in front and in line with the lower meniscus of water; looking from above or below gives an incorrect reading.

mistakes: Reading the top edge of water’s meniscus instead of its bottom edge.
Looking at the meniscus from above or below instead of keeping the eye level with it.
Taking a reading while the cylinder is tilted or held off a horizontal surface.
Giving the final liquid reading as the solid’s volume instead of subtracting the initial reading.
Forgetting that the overflow’s volume, not its mass, equals the solid’s volume in the displacement can method.
